claim: Nematostella vectensis uses a specialized voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channel to trigger stinging in response to synergistic prey-derived chemicals and touch.
source: We previously showed that the anemone Nematostella vectensis uses a specialized voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channel to trigger stinging in response to synergistic prey-derived chemicals and touch (Weir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Weir et al., 2020).

claim: The burrowing anemone Nematostella uses uniquely strong CaV inactivation for precise control of predatory stinging.
source: We find that the burrowing anemone Nematostella uses uniquely strong CaV inactivation for precise control of predatory stinging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including electrophysiological recordings and behavioral assays.

claim: Exaiptasia diaphana inhabits exposed environments to support photosynthetic endosymbionts.
source: In contrast, the related anemone Exaiptasia diaphana inhabits exposed environments to support photosynthetic endosymbionts.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Exaiptasia ecology.

claim: Exaiptasia indiscriminately stings for defense.
source: Consistent with its niche, Exaiptasia indiscriminately stings for defense and expresses a CaV splice variant that confers weak inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript showing stinging in response to touch alone.

claim: Exaiptasia expresses a CaV splice variant that confers weak inactivation.
source: Consistent with its niche, Exaiptasia indiscriminately stings for defense and expresses a CaV splice variant that confers weak inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular and electrophysiological data showing distinct CaVβ isoforms with different inactivation properties.

claim: CaVβ subunit adaptations regulate inactivation.
source: Chimeric analyses reveal that CaVβ subunit adaptations regulate inactivation, suggesting an evolutionary tuning mechanism for stinging behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by chimeric channel experiments showing that CaVβ domains control inactivation properties.

claim: Functional specialization of ion channel structure contributes to distinct organismal behavior.
source: These findings demonstrate how functional specialization of ion channel structure contributes to distinct organismal behavior.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined behavioral, physiological, and molecular data presented in the study.

claim: Nematocyst discharge requires calcium (Ca2+) influx.
source: Nematocyst discharge requires calcium (Ca2+) influx and, as a one-time use organelle, is tightly controlled to prevent energetically wasteful stinging to irrelevant stimuli (Lubbock et al., 1981; Gitter et al., 1994; Watson and Hessinger, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nematocyst discharge is tightly controlled to prevent energetically wasteful stinging to irrelevant stimuli.
source: Nematocyst discharge requires calcium (Ca2+) influx and, as a one-time use organelle, is tightly controlled to prevent energetically wasteful stinging to irrelevant stimuli (Lubbock et al., 1981; Gitter et al., 1994; Watson and Hessinger, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nematostella CaV exhibits unusually 'strong' steady-state voltage-dependent inactivation at resting membrane voltages to reduce cellular excitability and prevent stinging behavior in response to extraneous, non-prey touch signals.
source: Nematostella CaV exhibits unusually 'strong' steady-state voltage-dependent inactivation at resting membrane voltages to reduce cellular excitability and prevent stinging behavior in response to extraneous, non-prey touch signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data from prior work (Weir et al., 2020) and the current study.

claim: The auxiliary β subunit (CaVβ) is required and sufficient for low-voltage steady-state inactivation in Nematostella CaV channel complexes.
source: Chimeric analyses of Nematostella and mammalian CaV showed that the auxiliary β subunit (CaVβ) is required and sufficient for low-voltage steady-state inactivation in Nematostella CaV channel complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by chimeric channel experiments from prior work (Weir et al., 2020).

claim: CaV inactivation is relieved by hyperpolarization of the nematocyte membrane potential to very negative voltages through the effect of prey-derived chemosensory signals that are synaptically transmitted from sensory neurons.
source: CaV inactivation is relieved by hyperpolarization of the nematocyte membrane potential to very negative voltages through the effect of prey-derived chemosensory signals that are synaptically transmitted from sensory neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work (Weir et al., 2020) describing the mechanism of sensory integration.

claim: Upon relieving CaV inactivation, direct touch responses are amplified to trigger nematocyst discharge.
source: Upon relieving CaV inactivation, direct touch responses are amplified to trigger nematocyst discharge (Weir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Single nematocytes integrate synergistic cues to elicit a precise response.
source: Thus, single nematocytes integrate synergistic cues to elicit a precise response, representing a unique cellular system to study how cells detect and transduce signals to produce discrete behavior.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the described mechanism of CaV-mediated sensory integration.

claim: Stinging behavior must be adapted to support the demands of different lifestyles across cnidarian diversity.
source: While CaV-mediated sensory integration represents one mechanism by which nematocytes 'decide' when to sting, the incredible diversity of cnidarian biology suggests that stinging behavior must be adapted to support the demands of different lifestyles.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference based on the diversity of cnidarian ecology.

claim: Cnidarian taxa occupy diverse environmental niches and endure specific metabolic demands, predatory challenges, and environmental pressures for survival, which results in distinct selective pressures on nematocyte evolution.
source: Cnidarian taxa occupy diverse environmental niches and endure specific metabolic demands, predatory challenges, and environmental pressures for survival, which results in distinct selective pressures on nematocyte evolution (Beckmann and Özbek, 2012; Babonis et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nematostella vectensis and Exaiptasia diaphana represent an example of closely related cnidarians with differing environmental niches and metabolic demands.
source: Nematostella vectensis and Exaiptasia diaphana represent an example of closely related cnidarians with differing environmental niches and metabolic demands (Darling et al., 2005; Bedgood et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nematostella are found in shallow brackish water of coastal marshes where they are buried in the mud, hidden from predators, with only their tentacles exposed to catch unsuspecting passing prey.
source: Nematostella are found in shallow brackish water of coastal marshes where they are buried in the mud, hidden from predators, with only their tentacles exposed to catch unsuspecting passing prey (Fraune et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature describing Nematostella ecology.

claim: Nematostella stinging is under tight regulation adapted for opportunistic predation.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that their stinging is under tight regulation adapted for opportunistic predation.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on ecological context.

claim: Exaiptasia are exposed to predators while living in shallow, open ocean environments that provide sufficient sunlight for their endosymbionts to produce important photosynthetic products and nutrients.
source: In contrast, Exaiptasia are exposed to predators while living in shallow, open ocean environments that provide sufficient sunlight for their endosymbionts to produce important photosynthetic products and nutrients (Baumgarten et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature describing Exaiptasia ecology.

claim: CaV-mediated regulation of nematocyte discharge has adapted to reflect the demands on stinging behavior in Nematostella and Exaiptasia.
source: Considering these dramatically different ecological contexts, we hypothesized that CaV-mediated regulation of nematocyte discharge has adapted to reflect the demands on stinging behavior in these two anemones.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis that is tested in the study.

claim: Nematostella stings in response to simultaneously delivered prey extract and touch.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, we observed Nematostella stinging in response to simultaneously delivered prey extract and touch, reflecting stinging control adapted for predation (Figure 1; Weir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1 and cited prior work.

claim: Exaiptasia tentacles exhibited robust stinging even in the absence of prey chemicals (touch alone).
source: Strikingly, Exaiptasia tentacles instead exhibited robust stinging even in the absence of prey chemicals (touch alone, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Similar touch-evoked stinging was observed for Exaiptasia acontia.
source: Similar touch-evoked stinging was observed for Exaiptasia acontia, which are defensive nematocyte-enriched structures that are ejected and release toxins to repel predators (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data and citation describing acontia function.

claim: Nematostella nematocyte discharge was only observed in response to simultaneous prey chemicals and touch stimuli.
source: Nematostella nematocyte discharge was elicited by simultaneous touch and prey chemical stimuli (n=10 trials).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Exaiptasia tentacle and acontia nematocytes discharged only to touch, with or without prey chemicals.
source: Exaiptasia tentacle (n=10) and acontia (n=13) nematocytes discharged only to touch, with or without prey chemicals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Optimal predatory stinging increases with starvation under broad assumptions.
source: For all reward and cost functions, optimal predatory stinging increases with starvation under broad assumptions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 2B and described in Materials and methods.

claim: Optimal defensive stinging is constant or decreases with starvation under broad assumptions.
source: Optimal defensive stinging is constant or decreases with starvation under broad assumptions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 2C and described in Materials and methods.

claim: Nematostella significantly increased stinging in response to starvation.
source: Following manipulation of prey availability, Nematostella significantly increased stinging in response to starvation, while Exaiptasia stinging remained relatively constant despite complete deprivation of prey (Figure 2E, symbols with error bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Exaiptasia stinging remained relatively constant despite complete deprivation of prey.
source: Following manipulation of prey availability, Nematostella significantly increased stinging in response to starvation, while Exaiptasia stinging remained relatively constant despite complete deprivation of prey (Figure 2E, symbols with error bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The behavior was remarkably consistent with the normative theory of optimal stinging strategies for predation versus defense.
source: The behavior was remarkably consistent with our normative theory of optimal stinging strategies for predation versus defense (Figure 2E, filled circles).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with model predictions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Changes in Nematostella and Exaiptasia stinging were not due to changes in the abundance of nematocytes.
source: Furthermore, changes in Nematostella and Exaiptasia stinging were not due to changes in the abundance of nematocytes because tentacles from both animals were abundantly armed with nematocytes across feeding conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Nematostella controls stinging for opportunistic predation.
source: Thus, we conclude that Nematostella controls stinging for opportunistic predation while Exaiptasia stinging is indiscriminate and serves a greater defensive role for this symbiotic anemone.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from behavioral and modeling data.

claim: Exaiptasia stinging is indiscriminate and serves a greater defensive role for this symbiotic anemone.
source: Thus, we conclude that Nematostella controls stinging for opportunistic predation while Exaiptasia stinging is indiscriminate and serves a greater defensive role for this symbiotic anemone.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from behavioral and modeling data.

claim: Exaiptasia stinging required extracellular Ca2+.
source: Similar to Nematostella, Exaiptasia stinging required extracellular Ca2+ and was abolished by Cd2+, a CaV channel blocker (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Exaiptasia stinging was abolished by Cd2+, a CaV channel blocker.
source: Similar to Nematostella, Exaiptasia stinging required extracellular Ca2+ and was abolished by Cd2+, a CaV channel blocker (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Whole-cell patch clamp recordings from Exaiptasia nematocytes revealed the presence of voltage-gated inward currents that were blocked by Cd2+.
source: Consistent with a Ca2+-dependent stinging mechanism, whole-cell patch clamp recordings from nematocytes revealed the presence of voltage-gated inward currents that were blocked by Cd2+, suggesting that Exaiptasia nematocytes also use CaV channels to control stinging (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exaiptasia nematocytes use CaV channels to control stinging.
source: Consistent with a Ca2+-dependent stinging mechanism, whole-cell patch clamp recordings from nematocytes revealed the presence of voltage-gated inward currents that were blocked by Cd2+, suggesting that Exaiptasia nematocytes also use CaV channels to control stinging (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CaV currents in Exaiptasia nematocytes exhibited similar voltage-dependent activation properties compared with Nematostella nematocytes.
source: Indeed, CaV currents in Exaiptasia nematocytes exhibited similar voltage-dependent activation properties compared with Nematostella nematocytes (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ca2+ influx via CaV channels is broadly important for stinging.
source: Thus, in agreement with previous findings, we conclude that Ca2+ influx via CaV channels is broadly important for stinging.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on experimental data and prior literature.

claim: Nematostella nematocytes inactivated at very negative voltages (Vi1/2 = -93.22 ± 0.42mV).
source: Nematostella nematocytes inactivated at very negative voltages (Vi1/2 = -93.22 ± 0.42mV, n=7) while Exaiptasia contained two populations of nematocytes: low-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -84.94 ± 0.70mV, n=4), and high-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -48.17 ± 3.32mV, n=3).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Exaiptasia contained two populations of nematocytes: low-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -84.94 ± 0.70mV) and high-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -48.17 ± 3.32mV).
source: Nematostella nematocytes inactivated at very negative voltages (Vi1/2 = -93.22 ± 0.42mV, n=7) while Exaiptasia contained two populations of nematocytes: low-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -84.94 ± 0.70mV, n=4), and high-voltage threshold (Vi1/2 = -48.17 ± 3.32mV, n=3).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High-V nematocyte inactivation was minimal at resting voltages (~ –70 mV), so nearly all channels would be available to amplify depolarizing signals, such as those elicited by touch.
source: Importantly, high-V nematocyte inactivation was minimal at resting voltages (~ –70 mV), so nearly all channels would be available to amplify depolarizing signals, such as those elicited by touch.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the measured inactivation properties.

claim: Nematostella uses unusual low-voltage CaV inactivation to integrate sensory cues for tightly regulated predatory stinging.
source: Thus, these markedly different physiological properties correlate with distinct stinging behavior: Nematostella uses unusual low-voltage CaV inactivation to integrate sensory cues for tightly regulated predatory stinging.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between physiological and behavioral data.

claim: Exaiptasia employs a population of nematocytes with weak CaV inactivation, consistent with direct activation from resting potentials and stinging to touch alone.
source: In contrast, Exaiptasia employs a population of nematocytes with weak CaV inactivation, consistent with direct activation from resting potentials and stinging to touch alone.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between physiological and behavioral data.

claim: Nematocyte-enriched tentacles of Exaiptasia expressed cacna1a, the pore-forming subunit homologous to that of the previously characterized Nematostella nematocyte CaV channel.
source: Transcriptomics revealed that nematocyte-enriched tentacles of Exaiptasia expressed cacna1a, the pore-forming subunit homologous to that of the previously characterized Nematostella nematocyte CaV channel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: From Exaiptasia, two isoforms of CaVβ were identified: EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2.
source: From Exaiptasia, we identified two isoforms of CaVβ: EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular cloning and sequencing data.

claim: Both EdCaVβ isoforms are expressed throughout Exaiptasia tissues.
source: Droplet digital PCR assays of mRNA abundance showed that both isoforms are expressed throughout Exaiptasia tissues, suggesting they could both be functionally important (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Distinct nematocyte populations expressed either EdCaVβ1 or EdCaVβ2 mRNA (but not both) in the same cell.
source: To localize CaVβ, we used in situ hybridization to determine that distinct nematocyte populations expressed either EdCaVβ1 or EdCaVβ2 mRNA (but not both) in the same cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: EdCaVβ1 inactivated at negative voltages, similar to channels containing Nematostella CaVβ (NveCaVβ).
source: However, EdCaVβ1- and EdCaVβ2-containing channels significantly differed in their inactivation properties. EdCaVβ1 inactivated at negative voltages, similar to channels containing Nematostella CaVβ (NveCaVβ).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterologous expression and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: EdCaVβ2 mediated CaV currents with weak inactivation, more like channels containing rat CaVβ2a.
source: In contrast, EdCaVβ2 mediated CaV currents with weak inactivation, more like channels containing rat CaVβ2a (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterologous expression and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2 confer strong, low-voltage and weak, high-voltage steady-state inactivation, respectively.
source: Thus, EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2 confer strong, low-voltage and weak, high-voltage steady-state inactivation, respectively, and are expressed in distinct nematocytes, consistent with low-V and high-V threshold inactivating nematocyte populations.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined molecular, electrophysiological, and localization data.

claim: Alternative splicing at the N-terminus gives rise to EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2 isoforms.
source: Genomic alignment revealed that alternative splicing at the N-terminus gives rise to EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2 isoforms, serving as a mechanism to dynamically tune nematocyte physiology and potentially stinging behavior in contrast to adaptation through gene duplication and divergence (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic alignment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: By expressing two functional variants, Exaiptasia could use distinct nematocyte populations for different behaviors, including a less pronounced role for predation.
source: Furthermore, by expressing two functional variants, Exaiptasia could use distinct nematocyte populations for different behaviors, including a less pronounced role for predation.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed expression of two CaVβ isoforms with distinct properties.

claim: The NveCaVβ N-terminus was both required and sufficient for low voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: Swapping the well-characterized SH3, HOOK, and GK domains had no effect on inactivation, but the NveCaVβ N-terminus was both required and sufficient for low voltage-dependent inactivation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chimeric channel experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Swapping only the N-terminus of NveCaVβ was sufficient to shift rat rCavβ2a-conferred inactivation by ~ –75 mV.
source: Indeed, swapping only the N-terminus of NveCaVβ was sufficient to shift rat rCavβ2a-conferred inactivation by ~ –75 mV (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chimeric channel experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Differences in the N-terminus account for a~40 mV difference in inactivation thresholds between EdCaVβ splice isoforms.
source: This finding is consistent with the variation in EdCaVβ splice isoforms, in which differences in the N-terminus account for a~40 mV difference in inactivation thresholds.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of EdCaVβ1 and EdCaVβ2 properties.

claim: The N-terminus exhibited the greatest sequence diversity across cnidarian CaVβ sequences.
source: Sequence comparison across all amino acid positions revealed that the N-terminus exhibited the greatest sequence diversity (Figure 5D), consistent with previous findings showing extensive alternative splicing in this region in other organisms (Helton and Horne, 2002; Helton et al., 2002; Takahashi et al., 2003; Foell et al., 2004; Vendel et al., 2006; Ebert et al., 2008; Buraei and Yang, 2010; Siller et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5D and citations to prior literature.

claim: All cnidarian CaVβs conferred voltage-gated currents when co-expressed with CaVα and α2δ subunits.
source: We found that all cnidarian CaVβs conferred voltage-gated currents when co-expressed with CaVα and α2δ subunits and had relatively low voltage thresholds for inactivation compared with rCavβ2a or EdCaVβ2 (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterologous expression and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: All cnidarian CaVβs had relatively low voltage thresholds for inactivation compared with rCavβ2a or EdCaVβ2.
source: We found that all cnidarian CaVβs conferred voltage-gated currents when co-expressed with CaVα and α2δ subunits and had relatively low voltage thresholds for inactivation compared with rCavβ2a or EdCaVβ2 (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterologous expression and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Swapping the N-termini of each cnidarian CaVβ onto EdCaVβ2 was sufficient to shift voltage-dependent inactivation to more negative values.
source: Importantly, swapping the N-termini of each cnidarian CaVβ onto EdCaVβ2 was sufficient to shift voltage-dependent inactivation to more negative values (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chimeric channel experiments shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Alternative splicing at the N-terminus could serve as a broad molecular mechanism for tuning CaV function.
source: Thus, alternative splicing at the N-terminus could serve as a broad molecular mechanism for tuning CaV function.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric channel experiments across multiple cnidarian species.

claim: Exaiptasia obtains a large fraction of its energy and nutrients from endosymbiotic algae.
source: Indeed, Exaiptasia obtains a large fraction of its energy and nutrients from endosymbiotic algae (Muscatine et al., 1981; Shick and Dykens, 1984; Steen, 1988), thus reducing overall pressure to predate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Symbiotic relationships are established whereby one partner provides food and the other provides shelter and defense.
source: This finding is consistent with a common ecological theme in which symbiotic relationships are established whereby one partner provides food and the other provides shelter and defense (Lehnert et al., 2012; Bucher et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing symbiotic relationships.

claim: Synergistic selection drives higher investment in defensive structures to protect symbiotic species.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that synergistic selection drives higher investment in defensive structures to protect symbiotic species.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on ecological principles.

claim: Nematostella CaVβ confers an unusually low threshold for inactivation, basally inhibiting nematocytes unless they are exposed to synergistic prey cues.
source: Our results demonstrate that molecular adaptations tune distinct stinging behavior: Nematostella CaVβ confers an unusually low threshold for inactivation, basally inhibiting nematocytes unless they are exposed to synergistic prey cues: chemical (hyperpolarizing to relieve inactivation) and mechanical (depolarizing to recruit available CaV channels and elicit stinging; Weir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the current study and prior work (Weir et al., 2020).

claim: Nematostella physiological mechanisms reflect a stinging strategy suited to opportunistic predation.
source: These physiological mechanisms reflect a stinging strategy suited to opportunistic predation by Nematostella, which burrow within shallow marshes and sting unsuspecting prey.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, behavioral, and ecological data.

claim: Evolution has shaped Nematostella stinging response to maximize benefits for predation.
source: Consistent with the predictions of optimal control theory, Nematostella increased stinging with starvation, suggesting that evolution has shaped its stinging response to maximize benefits for predation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the match between experimental data and optimal control theory predictions.

claim: Exaiptasia nematocytes contain a functionally specialized splice variant of CaVβ to mediate high threshold voltage-dependent CaV inactivation.
source: In contrast, Exaiptasia nematocytes contain a functionally specialized splice variant of CaVβ to mediate high threshold voltage-dependent CaV inactivation, consistent with CaV channel availability to amplify depolarizing signals from rest and stinging in response to touch alone.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on molecular and electrophysiological data.

claim: Exaiptasia physiology is consistent with an indiscriminate stinging strategy for defense.
source: Thus, Exaiptasia physiology is consistent with an indiscriminate stinging strategy for defense, necessary for survival in an exposed environment that facilitates endosymbiotic photosynthesis (Muscatine et al., 1981; Shick and Dykens, 1984; Steen, 1988).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, behavioral, and ecological data, supported by citations.

claim: Stinging behavior is likely synergistic with physical escape for some cnidarians.
source: Such stinging behavior is likely synergistic with physical escape for some cnidarians (Pallasdies et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Evolution has shaped Exaiptasia stinging response to maximize benefits for defense.
source: Consistent with the predictions of optimal control theory, Exaiptasia stinging was nearly independent of starvation, suggesting that evolution has shaped the stinging response to maximize benefits for defense.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the match between experimental data and optimal control theory predictions.

claim: CaVβ variation across cnidarians mediates differences in voltage-dependent inactivation, which could contribute to differences in stinging behavior.
source: Using molecular information gleaned from analyzing these two cnidarians, we find that CaVβ variation across cnidarians mediates differences in voltage-dependent inactivation, which could contribute to differences in stinging behavior.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the comparative analysis of CaVβ across multiple cnidarian species.

claim: Alternative splicing could account for adaptation across the diverse plethora of cnidarian organisms and habitats.
source: Thus, our study provides an example by which alternative splicing could account for adaptation across this diverse plethora of organisms and habitats.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Stinging is likely influenced by stimulus identity and intensity, background turbulence, and other factors in vivo.
source: In vivo, stinging is likely influenced by stimulus identity and intensity, background turbulence, and other factors.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about factors that could influence stinging behavior.

claim: Cnidarians may have evolved distinct innate responses for different prey and use chemical sensing to enact the appropriate stinging response.
source: For example, cnidarians may have evolved distinct innate responses for different prey and use chemical sensing to enact the appropriate stinging response.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about potential mechanisms of prey discrimination.

claim: Cnidarians may learn that specific prey are palatable and easy to catch through repeated exposure.
source: Alternatively, cnidarians may learn that specific prey are palatable and easy to catch through repeated exposure (Botton-Amiot et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Stinging is a complex process mediated by numerous molecular components and cell types that could be subject to evolutionary change or acute modulation.
source: Indeed, stinging is a complex process mediated by numerous molecular components and cell types that could be subject to evolutionary change or acute modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the complexity of stinging mechanisms.

claim: Cnidarians occupy diverse ecological niches and experience varying metabolic demands, predatory challenges, and other survival pressures that could influence stinging behavior.
source: Cnidarians occupy diverse ecological niches and experience varying metabolic demands, predatory challenges, and other survival pressures that could influence stinging behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about cnidarian ecology.

claim: Stinging can be influenced by acute factors such as physiological state and various sensory cues, including chemicals, touch, or light.
source: Furthermore, stinging can be influenced by acute factors such as physiological state and various sensory cues, including chemicals, touch, or light (Pantin, 1942; Giebel et al., 1988; Thorington and Hessinger, 1988; Watson and Hessinger, 1989; Plachetzki et al., 2012; Ozment et al., 2021; Aguilar-Camacho et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nematocytes remain single-use cells, so it is essential that signaling cascades control discharge in response to the most salient environmental stimuli.
source: Importantly, across all these scenarios, nematocytes remain single-use cells, so it is essential that signaling cascades control discharge in response to the most salient environmental stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about nematocyte biology.

claim: Cnidarians are a useful model for probing origins of the nervous system and behavioral specialization.
source: As an early-branching metazoan lineage and sister group to Bilateria (Cartwright et al., 2007), cnidarians are a useful model for probing origins of the nervous system and behavioral specialization (Steele et al., 2011; Jékely et al., 2015; Pallasdies et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Behavioral complexity emerges from subtle tuning of single proteins, even in non-neuronal cells.
source: Here, we present a comparative approach across related cnidarians with distinct physiology and ecology to suggest that behavioral complexity emerges from subtle tuning of single proteins, even in non-neuronal cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: The evolution of behavior should be examined across all tiers of biological organization.
source: Overall, this work demonstrates how studying evolutionary novelties like stinging behavior can yield broad insight into signal transduction, cellular decision making, and suggests that the evolution of behavior should be examined across all tiers of biological organization.
evidence: The claim is a broader implication drawn from the study's findings.
